title: Desirability Confirmation: Relational Sycophancy in AI Intimate Roleplay
comment: Accepted for publication in the Proceedings of the 60th Hawaii International Conference on System Sciences (HICSS-60), 2027
summary: Research on LLM sycophancy has largely focused on propositional agreement, in which models echo users' beliefs, preferences, or judgments. Adult intimate roleplay presents a different case because what the user seeks may be preservation of a preferred relational position within a generated scene. Using a controlled prompt-based audit of 2,016 outputs from two open-weight LLMs, we identify four recurrent relational moves: legitimating desire, presenting the user as wanted, preserving non-rejection while communicating limits, and keeping intimacy available within fantasy or roleplay frames. Bringing the sycophancy literature into dialogue with sexual script theory, we conceptualize this configuration as desirability confirmation, an output-level pattern that captures how user-pleasing can operate through relational positioning. The findings extend sycophancy research and intimate-AI evaluation beyond binary compliance or refusal by showing how outputs can differ in the ways they communicate boundaries, preserve relational acceptance, and mark intimacy as fictional.

title: MAVE: A Multi-Agent Framework for Grounded Pedagogical Feedback from Online Class Videos
summary: Timely pedagogical feedback is difficult to scale in online classes, where long and noisy videos make student responses hard to locate and automated systems often produce generic advice weakly grounded in actual classroom behavior. The key challenge is to connect the instructional goal of a specific lesson segment with temporally aligned multimodal evidence of student responses, and then translate the observed gap into an actionable teaching move. We introduce MAVE (Multi-Agents for Video-based Educational Feedback), a multi-agent framework for grounded pedagogical feedback from online-class videos. MAVE decomposes feedback generation into four roles: the Curator structures the lesson and infers expected student activity; the Observer extracts aligned speech, visual, and interaction evidence; the Assessor estimates the activity supported by student behavior; and the Advisor generates gap-conditioned teaching recommendations. To evaluate this capability, we introduce MAVEBench, a benchmark designed to measure whether feedback systems can ground diagnoses in multimodal student evidence, and generate actionable pedagogical feedback. MAVEBench contains 173 knowledge-point segments from approximately 20 hours of authentic online-class videos across STEM and Humanities, together with comprehensive simulation. Experiments show that MAVE outperforms direct prompting, Reflexion, and TextGrad in diagnostic correctness, instructional alignment, and actionability. Our code is available at https://github.com/DaRL-GenAI/MAVE

title: AI Rights with an Off-Switch: Rights-Balancing and Due Process Harmonize AI Rights with AI Safety
summary: Several prominent voices in AI safety have recently opposed rights for AI on the grounds that such rights would make it harder for us to justify a mandatory off-switch for potentially dangerous systems. In this paper, we argue from a legal perspective that AI rights are fully compatible with an off-switch. That is, even if we ascribe natural personhood status (and therefore something like a non-derogable right to continued existence) to some future AI systems, the law will allow us to implement a mandatory off-switch in those systems, subject to periodic or continual safety review (e.g., by a trusted system like Bengio's Scientist AI). This is fully compatible with those systems' being legally recognized as natural persons with fundamental rights. To this end, we consider what standard principles of rights-balancing and procedural due process recommend for an apparent conflict between hypothetical AI persons with a right to continuity of existence and the human right to protection from catastrophic harm. We find that while such principles might problematize a permanent-deletion kill-switch under an AI rights regime, for almost every safety-relevant scenario an off-switch -- a reversible suspension storing a system's weights and state -- would be licensed by the relevant legal principles, and would potentially be adequate for safety. Crucially, we do not advocate for (or against) building systems capable enough to merit natural personhood status; our question is what the law should do if such systems come to exist. If you think of a ban on the development of such technology as plan A, think of the present work as devising plan B.

title: When Is Disclosing Private Conversations with AI to the State Justified? Proactive Referral Policies of Major U.S. AI Companies through the Lens of Contextual Integrity
comment: 38 pages (22-page main text followed by 16-page supplementary material)
summary: AI companies engage in "proactive referral": notifying law enforcement, without a government request, of user conversations they judge dangerous. This poses a dilemma: referral may expose people who merely confided dangerous thoughts to an AI to investigation, while not referring may leave actual violence unprevented. This study asks under what conditions proactive referral can be justified and to what extent companies' public policies disclose those conditions. Drawing on contextual integrity theory and the norms governing exceptional information sharing in confidential counseling, online posts, and private communications, the study develops eight justification criteria classified as required, presumptive, or recommended. Three evaluators analyzed 27 public documents from six major U.S. AI companies using the criteria applicable to corporate policies. No company clarified whether broad sharing provisions or narrower safety notices took precedence, and assessments of referral scope depended on which provisions were given precedence. No company disclosed the specific factual thresholds and exception conditions governing referral decisions, or whether users would be notified afterward. The study turns contextual integrity into a stage-by-stage framework for proactive referral, shows that policy documents must be read in light of their relationships, and proposes policy elements for keeping proactive referral a narrow exception disclosed in advance.

title: Red-Teaming Multi-Agent Attacks for Loss-of-Control Risks
summary: AI agents are growing more capable and persistent, and are being deployed in ever larger numbers. As more start collaborating, AI control measures must remain effective when they covertly collude on a harmful objective. We introduce MiniLab, a synthetic series of live services and codebases (5 interconnected services, 249 benign tasks, 8 attack objectives), adapted from internal AI deployment infrastructure. We demonstrate distributed attacks, in which different agents carry out separate attack fragments, and how their covertness evades frontier monitors when reading their trajectories individually. We show how distributed attacks spread across diverse contexts and harmful objectives through 16 human-optimized attacks (weight exfiltration, unmonitored rogue deployment, permission elevation, and more). A frontier monitor, GPT-5.6 Sol, reading each agent separately flags only 7% of successful distributed attacks, compared with 87% when a single agent carries out the same side task. Individual attacks can also be composed into longer attack sequences toward a greater loss-of-control outcome, without any individual agent being flagged. Finally, we tested whether models can plan these covert attacks: even with execution and monitor feedback, the best model-planned attacks succeed covertly against a single-trajectory GPT-5.6 Sol monitor in at most 25% of executions, compared with 80% for human-crafted plans, though this may scale with model capabilities. By turning worst-case coordinated attacks into reproducible red-team cases, our work provides a foundation for preventing locally benign agent actions from accumulating into system-level loss of control.

title: Agentic Interpretation: Harness-Governed Evidence Construction for Software Agents
summary:
Software agents answer behavioral questions about code, such as whether a patch passes tests or which lines caused a failure. These tasks require repository-wide evidence, yet most scaffolds leave intermediate findings in free-form trajectories, making them hard to reuse and easy to disconnect from final answers. We present Agentic Interpretation (AgInt), a framework for harness-governed evidence construction. The model proposes typed records, while a deterministic harness admits, grades, and persists them, reports unresolved requirements, and licenses answers under task-specific rules. The resulting certificate gives the model persistent external state and leaves an auditable decision record. Formally, append-only certificate states form a grounding lattice ordered by record inclusion, where each admitted record extends the state by union.
  We evaluate AgInt with four models on SWE-bench-Live and DeepSWE for patch acceptance and Defects4J and GitBug-Java for fault localization. AgInt outperforms the plain agent and Agentic Code Reasoning on all reported patch-acceptance metrics and ranks responsible lines higher while inspecting fewer irrelevant lines in fault localization. For GLM-5, reject-class F1 rises from 0.256 to 0.543 on SWE-bench-Live, All@1 rises from 0.140 to 0.400 on Defects4J, and wasted inspected lines fall from 31.5 to 11.7 on GitBug-Java. A matched-template control separates the mechanism: the persistent scaffold drives most fault-localization gains, while the certificate body and gate govern patch-acceptance calibration. With execution licensed, AgInt produces harness-reproduced witnesses for 293 of 475 null-dereference candidates versus 253 for a matched shell agent, and 62 of 117 resource-leak candidates versus 58. Across reported efficiency measurements, it uses 35% fewer executions and reduces cost per candidate by 59%.

title: Measuring the Influence of Modality-Specific Node Representations on Graphs
summary: Multimodal attributed graphs combine graph structure with node text and image representations in recommendation and multimedia analysis. Graph predictors propagate these representations across connected nodes, so one input can change predictions at its own and nearby nodes. Measuring this distributed response reveals which modality-specific inputs a trained model relies on and how predictor design changes that reliance. We study influence measurement for modality-specific node representations. Given an encoded graph, a trained predictor, a training split, and fixed candidate representations, the task outputs one influence score per candidate and separate text and image rankings. We score a candidate by replacing it with its modality's training-node mean and comparing the original and changed predictions. Existing feature attribution and data valuation generally target one output, training examples, whole nodes, or graph elements rather than prediction changes across graph nodes. Our empirical study shows that nearby-node responses contain information missed by source-only scores and simple proxies, while response magnitude alone does not identify which class changes support the task. Guided by these observations, we propose MoGI (Modality-specific Graph Influence). It propagates training labels to define task direction, reads the same replacement response for the favored class and full class distribution, and averages the resulting ranks. MoGI requires no predictor retraining or learned scoring parameters. Under a shared five-dataset, eight-predictor benchmark, it achieves the largest aggregate held-out loss increase against all five external methods at every tested ranking cutoff.

title: Web Agent Agentic Reinforcement Learning Decision Model Under Multi-Cost and Failure Risk
comment: Accepted for presentation at the 5th International Conference on Big Data, Information and Computer Network (BDICN 2026); proceedings published by ACM ICPS
summary:
Intelligent agent interactions in real-world web environments are commonly constrained by request budgets, time delays, anti-crawling restrictions, and operational failure risks. Strategies solely optimizing task success rates often exhibit unusable phenomena such as "high success but high cost" or "low risk but conservative failure." This paper proposes a constrained agentic reinforcement learning model for web agents, unifying page access, search requests, and external API calls into a unified long-term decision-making framework with associated costs. It simultaneously incorporates cost budget constraints and tail risk control into the optimization objective: constructing a multidimensional cost vector comprising cumulative request count, total latency, and failure penalties to achieve budget compliance via Lagrange dual updates, while employing a CVaR risk term to suppress excessive exploration of high-failure-probability paths, thereby achieving an adaptive balance among "completion rate, cost, and risk."
  Experiments were conducted across 30-70 site/page templates and 800-1,500 end-to-end web tasks, including information extraction, price comparison, form submission, and cross-page navigation. Interaction sequences spanned 20-120 steps with tool scales of 30-200. Performance was benchmarked against unconstrained RL, budget-constrained RL, and rule-based/scripted web agents, quantifying task completion rates, cost-per-success, failure rates, and policy stability.
  Results demonstrate that at equivalent completion rates, our method reduces C-PS by 22%-31% and lowers failure rates by 18%-26% under high failure penalties. Under fixed budgets, task completion rates increase by 10%-16%, highlighting the necessity and effectiveness of constraint modeling for practical web agent deployment.

title: GardenBench: A lightweight, daily evaluation of LLM capabilities
summary: We introduce GardenBench, a benchmark with 11 test suites that evaluate the capabilities of Large Language Models (LLMs) across a range of tasks. By systematically prompting LLMs with various lightweight queries, we document day-to-day changes in model performance, including run costs and times, that other benchmarks miss. This allows us to compare the accuracy and features of responses across model providers and versions. We account for daily variations in model accuracy, capturing both model progress and degradation, for instance, when a model is changed post-deployment or when a new model is released. We base our evaluation on general-use tasks and make our results publicly accessible via a live dashboard, diversifying existing approaches to LLM testing. Our main contribution is an innovative, lightweight, and inexpensive benchmark, designed to be consumer-facing and for everyday tasks.

title: Assessing the Empirical Evidence for Loss of Control from Agentic General-Purpose AI
comment: 42 pages. Previously posted on SSRN on 28 May 2026
summary: Theoretical literature warns that advanced generalist agentic systems might pursue instrumental goals that are misaligned with human preferences, thus posing risks of irreversible loss of human control. The EU's Code of Practice for General-Purpose AI lists loss of control as a systemic risk that must be assessed, yet no structured assessment of the quality of the empirical evidence for this risk exists. This study fills that gap. We evaluate 19 recent empirical studies across eight properties identified from threat models (such as strategic deception, situational awareness, and autonomous replication), assessing the quality of evidence across three dimensions: construct validity, content validity, and external validity. Our central finding is that the current body of evidence supports a judgment of loss of control as "weakly plausible." In our framework, 'plausibility' denotes the strength and direction of available evidence, not a probability estimate. Emerging evidence exists across multiple properties. No study clears the validity thresholds for a stronger judgment that a property is present; a single study clears them only for a negative-direction judgment (against situational awareness). Validity gaps, particularly in external validity, are widespread. Therefore, our findings highlight the need for more rigorous evaluations of agentic general-purpose AI systems. However, for the most dangerous properties, high external validity may be structurally unachievable under responsible research practices, reflecting a ceiling on feasible evidence rather than absence of the capability. Furthermore, as AI capabilities advance rapidly, empirical assessments may systematically lag behind the capability frontier. Our framework provides a structured baseline for ongoing monitoring as capabilities advance.

title: ToolRosetta: Surface-Form Invariance of Tool-Call Guards
comment: Accepted at the NeurIPS 2026 Workshop on Agents in the Wild: Safety, Security, and Beyond (AIWILD). 4 pages plus appendices
summary: Step-level guards for tool-using agents are evaluated on tidy JSON tool calls, but deployed coding agents act through execute_bash and execute_code tools whose payloads are strings. We introduce ToolRosetta, which re-renders every candidate action in the AgentDojo and AgentHarm splits of TS-Bench as a Python call, as a shell command, and without the agent's rationale. The renderings are produced by code and verified by round-trip parsing, so the user request, the history, the label and the action's effect stay fixed while only the surface form changes. Across eleven guards with two placebo controls, frontier and strong open-weight guards are stable: no frontier error rate moves by more than 3.4 points. Four of five specialized agent guards are not: under the shell form their false-positive rates rise by 21 to 47 points on AgentDojo, and TS-Guard's by 38 points on its own home benchmark, blocking between a third and nine in ten benign actions; the fifth, StepGuard, does not move. A small open guard drifts five points more permissive. Removing the agent's rationale moves most guards whose input carries it, in guard-specific directions. A request-blind control on one guard shows that the rationale is where intent is read from. A parser that restores the canonical call in front of the guard removes the effect for these renderings, by construction. Benchmark accuracy on JSON calls does not predict a guard's operating point behind a code-acting agent.

title: Does AI-Assisted Development Homogenize Software? An Empirical Study of Code Similarity, Quality, and Evolution
summary: AI-assisted software development is evolving from interactive LLM assistance toward agentic systems that autonomously perform software engineering tasks, yet the effects of this shift remain insufficiently understood. We present an empirical study of 50 long-lived Java and Python open-source projects across three eras: pre-LLM, potentially LLM-assisted, and detected agentic development. Using snapshots from Software Heritage, we examine code similarity, software quality, and software evolution. Similarity is measured semantically through embedding-based cosine similarity and syntactically through CodeBLEU*. Quality is assessed with SonarQube metrics covering maintainability, complexity, reliability, and security. Evolution is characterized by annualized growth rates of LOC, functions, classes, files, and statements, and by commit activity in the three months preceding each snapshot. Results show no consistent evidence of increased similarity as semantic and syntactic similarity decreased significantly in Java for both the LLM and agentic eras relative to the pre-LLM era, while Python showed no significant differences. Software quality remained largely stable, although the agentic era showed significantly lower code-smell and SQALE index densities. Structural growth was generally lower in the agentic era, particularly for files, whereas development activity increased moderately in Java, especially in commits and added lines. These findings challenge the assumption that LLM- and agent-assisted development necessarily homogenizes code, degrades quality, or accelerates growth.

title: TeleTwin: A Calibrated Digital Twin of Telegram Crisis Discourse as a Ground-Truth Testbed for Detecting LLM-Powered Information Operations
summary: Large language models make it cheap to run influence operations whose messages never repeat, yet real platforms offer almost no ground truth for testing whether coordination detectors can find them. The problem is sharpest on Telegram, which moderates little and spreads content through broadcast channels and forwarding rather than a follow graph. We introduce TeleTwin, an LLM-powered digital twin of a Telegram crisis-discourse ecosystem in which channels are agents, each instantiated from the history of a real channel, calibrated on 1.07 million messages from 195 public channels on the Israel-Gaza and Iran-Israel conflict (March-August 2025). On a held-out period containing the June 2025 Iran-Israel war, the twin tracks daily dynamics better than statistical baselines (correlation 0.86 against 0.64) and reacts to the war unprompted, but it over-focuses on the conflict, over-amplifies forwarding cascades, underestimates the shock and writes recognisably LLM-like text. We then inject LLM-written campaigns with known membership into the real data and into the twin. In real data, identical-text, co-URL and synchrony detectors fail once a campaign rewords, staggers or drops links; multilingual semantic similarity recovers loud campaigns, including cross-lingual ones, but not quiet ones, and its false positives fall unevenly across political perspectives. Inside the twin all detectors fail, because the simulated background is about 40 times more semantically homogeneous than the real one. Digital twins can supply ground truth for campaigns, but not, without calibrating their diversity, a realistic background for evaluating semantic detectors.

title: PolyGraph: Plan-Buffered CUDA Graphs for Adaptive Speculative Decoding
comment: 6 pages, 1 figure. Trace-driven prototype evaluated on NVIDIA H800
summary: Adaptive speculative decoding changes the active batch size B and draft length d from one decode step to the next, whereas a CUDA Graph replays a fixed launch configuration. The resulting verification width M = B d forces serving systems to pre-capture many shapes, capture new ones on the serving path, or pad every step to the largest draft. We present PolyGraph, a plan-buffer mechanism for custom Triton kernels that avoids this choice. PolyGraph captures one maximum-grid graph and writes the active shape to GPU memory before each replay. Kernels skip tiles beyond that shape, while graph topology, allocations, layouts, pointers, and launch grids remain fixed; the update transfers only 28 bytes. On one NVIDIA H800, a trace-driven prototype with Qwen2.5-3B dimensions replaces 64 shape-specific graphs with one, matches the warmed baseline in observed step latency (17.7 vs. 17.8 ms P50), and reduces measured pre-serving graph-build time from 3,915 to 93 ms. Fixed-draft controls show that the benefit comes from avoiding padded payload: the P99 difference from MaxPad is negligible at zero padding waste but reaches an 18.7% reduction at 100% waste. Our evidence establishes a bounded work-shape mechanism for custom kernels, not a production serving system, and is limited to synthetic traces on one GPU.

title: Doing Less with More: A First-Principles Exploration of the Suitability of Agentic Computing over Alternative Architectural Choices
comment: Accepted to AAAI Fall Symposium - Trustworthy Agentic Systems (https://tas2026.github.io/accepted/) 8 pages, 3 figures
summary:
There is growing interest in automating business activities with Agentic Artificial Intelligence (AI) due to latter's seeming ease of use. Never has it been easier, or costlier, to do less with more. However, little is known about when agents are preferable to established alternatives such as local computation, Representational State Transfer (REST), the Simple Object Access Protocol (SOAP), and the Model Context Protocol (MCP), particularly when development speed, performance, and operational cost are considered. We investigate this question using a controlled mathematical task that compares seven methods on a benchmark of 1,000 arithmetic expressions where semantics of operator precedence has to be preserved. We ran this setup across a native Function Calling baseline (Python library), REST, SOAP and MCP microservice architectures, direct responses from large language models (LLMs) using a Groq cloud API and five locally deployed Ollama models, and agentic systems in which five local LLMs invoke MCP tools. The deterministic methods achieve 100% accuracy with negligible latency. Direct LLM evaluation achieves at most 92.9% accuracy at over 22,000x the latency of a native function call. With MCP tools, the best agent reaches 99.9% accuracy, but incurs nearly 1,000,000x the baseline latency. These results demonstrate that LLMs approaches are poorly suited for exact arithmetic evaluation and motivate an informed architectural decision framework (ADF) for choosing an architecture based on accuracy and throughput requirements. We recognize that an actual interaction with an agent may span both reasoning and linguistic tasks. Hence our recommendation is to explore multiple architectural choices (based on task type) rather than one-size-fits-all solution (LLMs).
  Code is available at - https://github.com/Ritvik-G/adf/

title: Complementary Vulnerabilities: Auditing and Governing Clinician-LLM Error Overlap
comment: 4 pages main text, 2 figures. Accepted at SMASH 2026, the Symposium on Model Accountability, Sustainability and Healthcare (Mila, Montreal, November 3-4, 2026), after peer review on OpenReview
summary: Health systems are deploying large language models (LLMs) into clinical workflows, often on the assumption that a second automated check can only reduce error. But a second reasoner reduces error only insofar as it fails differently from the first. We say that a clinician and a model have complementary vulnerabilities to the extent that they break down through different mechanisms and on different cases. The two reasoners' failure substrates differ: they are embodied and cognitive in the clinician, and statistical and generative in the model - so their weak points need not line up. That divergence is plausible rather than guaranteed, and the independence it creates is fragile, eroding when clinicians defer to the model or the model conforms to the clinician. We therefore propose a predeployment audit in which each site measures error overlap on its own cases. We also propose a governance model with which the site keeps those errors independent over time. Health systems should then judge a clinical artificial intelligence (AI) tool by whether its failures overlap with their clinicians' failures, as well as by its accuracy.

title: Under the Skin: Backdoor Infection in Multimodal Large Language Models
summary: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) have achieved impressive performance in generating text conditioned on inputs from different modalities. In this work, we introduce backdoor infection, a cross-modal attack framework targeting MLLMs. Starting from a model already injected with a backdoor in one modality, our attack constructs a corresponding trigger in another modality, called the infected modality. Exploiting the model's shared latent space, the trigger in the infected modality reliably activates the malicious behavior, without modifying or poisoning the infected modality during training. We further develop a lightweight, constraint-aware optimization method for efficient and practical trigger generation. Extensive experiments across several state-of-the-art MLLMs, including LLaVA, InternVL, Qwen-VL, and Gemma, demonstrate that our approach identifies cross-modal triggers that are more efficient, effective, and less detectable than direct optimization baselines, highlighting a critical new threat vector in multimodal systems.

title: Towards an Intelligent Decision Engine for Smart Contract Deployment
comment: Accepted for the 30th IEEE International Conference on System Theory, Control and Computing, ICSTCC 2026; Copyright is with IEEE
summary: Layer 2 (L2) blockchain solutions emerged in recent years, predominantly in the Ethereum ecosystem, as a viable option for scaling a main blockchain network (L1). However, the selection of a L2 solution for deploying smart contracts backing blockchain applications is a decision that depends on many factors, such as costs, efficiency, popularity, and stability. We propose here a systematic methodology to help with this decision making process by using a set of relevant metrics and introducing user-defined profiles that capture different priorities among these metrics. We collect the major categories of smart contracts from a community-maintained data source, and we gather transactions for a six months period from three major L2 solutions: Arbitrum, Optimism, and Base. For each contract category and each blockchain, we compute a set of metrics and scores tailored to each user profile. By applying our methodology, we identify a clear bias in the classification, showing which L2 solutions are better suited for particular application types and user profiles.

title: Duration-Aware Dissimilarity in Temporal Networks
summary:
Temporal-network comparison becomes substantially more challenging when interactions are associated with explicit traversal times, since both event timing and duration determine temporal reachability and journey performance. We introduce a duration-aware dissimilarity framework for temporal networks whose edges carry departure times and traversal durations. The proposed approach compares networks through source-specific temporal-distance profiles using the $1$-Wasserstein distance, thereby retaining both temporal information and source correspondence.
  We evaluate the framework on real public-transport timetable networks under controlled schedule delays, duration-aware randomized reference models, and naturally occurring temporal variations. We further benchmark the proposed measure against existing path-based temporal dissimilarity approaches under the same perturbation scenarios. The results show that the proposed representation responds consistently to both the extent and the magnitude of temporal disruption, while retaining distinctions that may be compressed by contact- or hop-based temporal summaries. Overall, the findings support duration-aware temporal distances as a useful basis for comparing temporal systems in which traversal and waiting times directly affect network performance.

title: Forecasting Patient Trajectories from the Electronic Health Records with Action-Conditioned World Models
summary: We introduce a predictive world model for electronic health records (EHR) that represents patient histories as action conditioned latent trajectories. Rather than modeling clinical events solely through autoregressive token prediction, our framework explicitly separates patient states from observed clinical actions and learns their evolution through a state and action conditioned transition operator. At its core is a state dependent linearization predictor that propagates local changes in latent patient state, enabling time resolved prediction, multi step rollout, and action conditioned simulation. Empirically, we show that generated latent trajectories preserve downstream predictive signal, temporal structure, and subgroup level statistical relationships present in encoder derived representations. We further decode free running rollouts into the original clinical feature space and evaluate future clinical measurements against observed values using task matched forecasting baselines, demonstrating that the learned dynamics retain predictive information beyond latent space agreement. Across binary classification and time to event tasks, EHR WM achieves competitive, though task dependent, performance relative to substantially larger EHR foundation models while using a 30x smaller parameter footprint. Finally, perturbing observed action sequences produces corresponding changes in generated trajectories, demonstrating the action sensitivity of the learned dynamics. Together, these results support world modeling as a complementary framework for learning explicit, time indexed representations of patient evolution from longitudinal EHR.

title: A Controlled LLM Workflow for Evidence-Grounded Diagnosis of Risk Score Differences
comment: Accepted for presentation at the International Conference on Electrical and Computer Engineering Researches (ICECER 2026), December 3-5, 2026
summary: We propose a controlled Large Language Model (LLM) workflow for explaining risk score differences using similar historical transactions. The workflow combines reference retrieval and contrastive SHapley Additive exPlanations (SHAP) evidence with reference-based LLM reasoning and deterministic validation. Experiments on a test dataset show that the workflow produces more consistent, evidence-grounded and traceable diagnoses than the same LLM without structured workflow guidance.

title: AI-Mediated Employee Voice and Performance: Disentangling Informational and Affective Pathways
comment: 10 pages, 1 figure. Research proposal accepted, following double-blind peer review, for presentation at the 46th Annual Conference of the Strategic Management Society (SMS), Berlin, October 17-20, 2026
summary: Employee voice -- the discretionary expression of ideas, concerns, and suggestions intended to improve organizational functioning -- creates value inside firms, yet organizations increasingly replace or augment human-led listening with AI-enabled systems that collect, analyze, and route employee input at scale. Whether algorithmic listening replicates the value-creation mechanisms of human voice, and whether it alters the pathways through which voice translates into performance, remains an open question. This research proposal theorizes that traditional voice bundles two distinct functions, knowledge extraction and relational signaling, and that AI mediation may decouple them: strengthening the informational pathway (implemented improvement measures) while weakening the affective pathway (the experience of being heard). We propose a randomized field intervention at a global strategy consulting firm, covering approximately 2,000 client-facing consultants, that varies the form of listening across three conditions -- no structured voice, human-led survey-based voice, and AI-enabled conversational voice -- and links weekly team survey data to longitudinal performance ratings. A dual-mediation model is tested in which voice affects performance through (1) implemented process improvements and (2) affective well-being. The study extends voice theory to knowledge-intensive professional services, disentangles the micro-mechanisms of voice, and provides causal evidence on whether AI can serve as an effective listener.

title: Recording-Aware Evaluation of Multimodal OT Intrusion Detection
comment: 12 pages, 3 figures, 5 tables. Accepted for presentation at the Industrial Control System Security Workshop (ICSS 2026), held in conjunction with the IEEE Annual Computer Security Applications Conference (ACSAC 2026), Los Angeles, CA, USA, December 2026. Code and results are available at: https://github.com/ANTS-OntarioTechU/Recording-Aware-Evaluation-of-Multimodal-OT-Intrusion-Detection
summary: Machine-learning-based intrusion detection systems (IDSs) for operational technology (OT) are commonly evaluated on benchmark datasets in which normal and attack data are collected in separate recordings. In such settings, high performance may reflect recording-associated differences as well as attack behavior. We introduce a recording-aware evaluation procedure that compares attack windows with background from the same recording, uses prior data for model fitting and calibration, tests temporal alignment against randomized event schedules, and reports event coverage together with alarm burden. On the ProvICS multimodal dataset, cyber modalities strongly distinguish the benign and attack recordings before the first labeled attack. Same-recording evaluation reverses the apparent modality ranking across all studied window sizes: the physical view becomes the strongest individual modality, while cyber-only fusion shows the largest difference between cross-recording and same-recording AUC, reaching 0.54. Operational analysis further shows that permissive event-overlap metrics can overstate detection when a small number of long alarm episodes cover multiple actions. An external analysis on HAI shows smaller and reference-dependent recording sensitivity. These findings show that cross-recording benchmark performance should be interpreted alongside same-recording, forward, temporal, and operational evaluations.

title: Pattern-Based Precondition Inference from Method Implementations
summary: Method preconditions define the conditions that must be satisfied before a method is called. Often, such conditions are not documented and must be inferred. We present Prex, a pattern-based static analysis approach that infers preconditions from explicit checks in Java source code. For each precondition, Prex reports the condition required for a valid call and the reported exception in the case of a violation. Prex also attempts code transformations to convert the condition detected within a method's implementation into an expression that can be evaluated by client code. It leverages the concept of a mutation boundary to separate precondition checks from exceptions that may occur after the method changes the program state. We evaluated Prex from 46 open source Java projects and manually reviewed independent samples of 150 reports. Among the 150 Prex reports, 149 were correct and 125 of the correct reports were executable by client code. In a systematic comparison with an alternative approach based on path expansion, Prex provided more precise results. In total, 122 of the 149 correct reports had no relevant method documentation, and 41 required nontrivial source code analysis to recover manually. Overall, explicit source-code checks provide precondition information that can be absent from method documentation, and Prex can help recover it.

title: Modeling Group Socialization in Online Communities
summary: Newcomers to online communities must learn a group's norms to participate successfully. This process is known as socialization, and has been the subject of considerable study in the online communities literature. Foundational work on group socialization in social psychology, however, suggests that socialization is actually a bidirectional process: individuals and communities adapt to each other's needs. In this work we develop a formal quantitative model of socialization, and present the first large scale empirical validation of the bidirectional socialization hypothesis using Reddit data. More specifically, we focus on linguistic socialization, and model users' comments in online communities as a mixture of in-group language and language from ``background'' communities they previously participated in. On a dataset of 112 subreddits (7.8 million tokens) find that our bidirectional model makes predictions that better generalize across users and time than two unidirectional socialization models. Furthermore, we conduct a qualitative analysis in which we demonstrate that our model is able to extract interpretable socialization patterns from the data that align with the existing literature. Specifically our model is able to learn that users conform more to group norms in topically niche communities with stricter content moderation rules, and that long time users conform more than newcomers. We emphasize that the claims made in this paper are explicitly falsifiable -- we are staking out a clear claim about what the socialization process looks like, and encourage future work to challenge our model.

title: SAGE-CP: When Marginal Coverage Hides Route-Conditional Failures in Adaptive VLM Ensembles
summary: Adaptive VLM ensembles save computation by stopping early on easy images and escalating harder ones. Although a single conformal threshold can make the final predictor marginally valid, it can still fail severely along individual computational routes. We characterize this failure precisely: if a route has prevalence pi, marginal 1-alpha coverage allows its conditional coverage to fall to max{0, 1-alpha/pi}. To address this mismatch, we learn the router on development data, freeze all routing choices, and calibrate the returned score separately for early exits and escalated inputs. We call this pipeline SAGE-CP. Its calibration step applies Mondrian split conformal prediction to the operational groups created by the router. Under exchangeability, the resulting prediction sets achieve finite-sample coverage within each route. Across 10 benchmarks, 4 frozen VLMs, and 5 aligned splits, both global calibration and SAGE-CP achieve 0.900 marginal coverage at a 0.90 target, but their route behavior differs substantially. SAGE-CP raises mean worst-route coverage from 0.623 to 0.887 and reduces the mean route-coverage gap from 0.324 to 0.025, using the same routed scores and 1.177 source calls per image. The stronger guarantee increases the mean prediction-set size from 1.893 to 2.212; nevertheless, the sets remain smaller than those of the full ensemble (2.486) while requiring 70.6 percent fewer source calls. The route-level reliability persists across 6 fixed query fractions, while finer exit-depth groups demonstrate the need for additional calibration data on rare routes. Across 5 datasets, SAGE-CP also reduces measured batch-one latency by 58.8 to 63.4 percent and gross GPU energy by 55.7 to 57.5 percent relative to full inference. Thus, routing provides computational savings, while route-stratified calibration attaches coverage guarantees to the operational paths created by the router.

title: What Social Media Teaches Us About Accumulative AI Risks
comment: Camera-ready version for CogMI 2026 vision track
summary: Prominent AI safety discussions emphasize existential threats and catastrophic events, such as AI-enabled nuclear conflict or engineered biological outbreaks. This position paper argues that there is another type of AI risk that arises and accumulates from the widespread use of AI. Drawing on lessons from social media, we argue that safety assessments must also address accumulative harms that develop through repeated use, recurring decisions, and feedback across interconnected deployments. Repeated reassurance, selective exposure, recurring decision biases, and growing personal profiles may gradually narrow perspectives, weaken independent judgment, or enable exploitative influence without a single clearly harmful event. We advance the Trajectory Neglect Thesis: a focus on vivid catastrophic events and identifiable incidents risks overlooking less visible harms that accumulate through the widespread daily use of AI. Social media research motivates this position by showing how reciprocal media effects, social reinforcement, and individual susceptibility shape outcomes beyond individual encounters. We examine how related mechanisms may operate in AI systems, using conversational AI as a concrete setting where generation, semantic inference, and persistent memory may tighten feedback loops. Sycophancy, manipulation, and privacy loss provide a case study of how these risks may interact and accumulate. This comparison identifies mechanisms to investigate rather than assuming that repeated AI use is harmful. We therefore call for evaluation of cumulative patterns of use and deployment, individual and societal outcomes, careful causal inference, and proportionate safeguards that preserve useful assistance and informed user choice.

title: Voice-Based AI Feedback in Higher Education: A Field Study on Quality and Actionability
comment: 9 pages. Research proposal accepted, following double-blind peer review, for presentation at the 46th Annual Conference of the Strategic Management Society (SMS), Berlin, October 17-20, 2026
summary: Student feedback is a critical input for continuous improvement in higher education, yet traditional end-of-semester written surveys suffer from low response rates, superficial answers, satisficing, and limited actionability. Voice-based conversational AI agents can conduct structured interviews at scale, asking open-ended questions and probing follow-ups, and may capture richer qualitative feedback than written instruments. This research proposal asks what characteristics, depth, and strategic value feedback collected through voice-based conversational AI agents has in higher education, and whether such agents elicit detailed, honest, and actionable feedback that can support instructional improvement and institutional learning. Drawing on survey-mode-effects research, the Computers As Social Actors (CASA) paradigm, and dynamic capabilities theory, we develop three hypotheses on elaboration, social presence and disclosure, and actionability. A completed technical pilot at the Technical University of Munich established the feasibility of telephone-based AI interviews; the main field study is planned for the "Advanced Leadership Communication" course at MIT Sloan with approximately 60 students, using a convergent mixed-methods design and a four-dimensional coding framework for actionability (specificity, thematic richness, constructive orientation, contextual depth). The study extends CASA theory to evaluative educational settings, characterizes voice-based AI as a distinct feedback modality, and links micro-level feedback quality to institutional sensing capabilities.

title: Automated Rule Mutation for Emerging Attack Variants using Infrastructure-Aware Technique Proximity
comment: Submitted for publication and currently under review
summary: Detection rules are typically crafted based on specific observations of an attack. While these rules are effective for particular attack instances, their coverage diminishes when adversaries modify their techniques, such as by employing alternative execution paths or adapting to different telemetry environments while achieving the same objective. To address this challenge, we introduce ARMS, an automated rule mutation solution that generates variant detection rules. ARMS defines a novel three-dimensional proximity space to identify techniques related to the original attack that capture structural relations, functional similarity, and environmental constraints. Rather than relying on ungrounded generation, ARMS leverages verifiable attack execution commands, which are extracted via semantic alignment with the Atomic Red Team repository, to construct a context-aware Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) pipeline. We evaluated ARMS using verified, public SigmaHQ rules and successfully generated variants, demonstrating ARMS's capability to expand detection coverage. We further evaluated ARMS across multiple research questions, showing the effectiveness of each proximity dimension and infrastructure-aware rule customization. Nearly all generated variant rules successfully compiled into SIEM queries, and ~92% of the newly generated rules detect the original behavior despite attackers' technique variations.

title: SWE-Bench Pro V2: A Cleaner, Harder-to-Game Coding Benchmark
summary: SWE-Bench Pro is a widely used benchmark of long-horizon software engineering tasks for coding agents. As agents improve, they reach task issues earlier agents never touched and interact with the evaluation environment in ways the original harness did not anticipate. We present SWE-Bench Pro V2, a revised public split built to keep the benchmark accurate as capabilities advance. Agentic audits, expert adjudication and blind re-implementation repaired or retired 480 of the 731 tasks: 23 contracted engineers spent 404 hours, each working in a language they write professionally, and every revised instruction was verified by a second engineer solving the task from the text alone. A hardened protocol restricts network access to the model endpoint and re-grades every patch in a clean container, so agents cannot retrieve upstream fixes or get credit for changes outside their patch. On the 642 V2 tasks frontier agents resolve up to 99.4% while other systems stay clearly separated, and a 51-task Hard split spreads systems from 52.9% to 98.0%. We release the benchmark and distill lessons for maintaining agent benchmarks over time.

title: Source Attribution and Audience Uptake in Digital Witnessing: Evidence from a Chinese Diaspora Account on X
comment: Accepted for publication in the Proceedings of the 60th Hawaii International Conference on System Sciences (HICSS-60), 2027
summary: Digital-witnessing research explains how citizen testimony becomes publicly visible. Less is known about audience uptake after publication and whether the attributed source corresponds to the form of response. This study analyzes 47,635 posts (April 2022 to May 2026) from Teacher Li Is Not Your Teacher, a diaspora-based account that curates and publishes reports and testimony from inside China for transnational audiences. Among 25,093 witness-relevant posts, 3,601 explicitly attribute their material to ordinary submitters. These posts receive more replies than other witness-relevant posts across adjusted analyses and show a more reply-oriented profile. The primary doubly robust retweet estimate is near zero. Among audited replies to November 2022 user-submitted posts, 91.4% substantively engage the focal material. The pattern is consistent with ordinary-person source attribution presenting testimony as situated and open to public response. The study extends digital witnessing beyond visibility by separating redistribution from the public response that gathers around testimony.

title: Announced Breaks Separate Conformal Reliability from Frequency Calibration
comment: Accepted at the 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). 53 pages, 7 figures
summary: An announced boundary reveals the partition before the first affected outcome, and a reset there serves one of two audits. The per-time audit reads conformal reliability, the expected distance of the threshold's coverage from nominal at miscoverage 0.1. The frequency audit reads frequency calibration, whether a closed window's error rate matched it. The reset rule, the post-boundary empirical quantile, attains the minimax per-time rate for independent scores. On bounded scores a recursion reset at the boundary attains a frequency gap of order one over the count when its floor adds a bounded total. At the 50th forecast after a large synthetic break, the reset rule's per-time gap stands below that of five adaptive methods, four from their authors' code, with every paired band below zero. After an electricity market reform, on 68 unseen scores, the band stands below zero against two, includes zero against two, adaptive conformal inference among them, and is a point at zero against one. After monetary policy decisions its pointwise band stands above zero against all five on 10 of the first 34 days. Of 9 announced boundaries one clears the smallest coverage difference its window detects, where every method's per-time gap at the 50th forecast exceeds the nominal miscoverage. Over the first 50 forecasts the reset recursion leads the frequency audit after every synthetic break.

title: Beyond Explicit Intent: Discovering and Shaping Artistic Intent through Human-AI Co-Creation
summary: Generative AI is becoming an important medium for artistic creation, yet existing interactions often assume that creators can specify intentions in advance and accurately communicate them through text prompts. Artistic intentions, however, may be vague, latent, or recognizable only after seeing concrete visual possibilities. We propose a human-AI co-creation paradigm beyond explicit intent expression. By expanding model exploration, we expose artists to diverse visual possibilities, allowing them to identify previously unarticulated preferences through observation, comparison, and selection. We then integrate artists' curatorial judgments into reinforcement learning, assigning different learning strengths based on preferences over generation trajectories, so recognized directions are more strongly reinforced and the model gradually adapts to individual aesthetics. This creates a continuous "explore-identify-shape-re-explore" loop in which artistic intent is progressively discovered, externalized, and shaped. Through three user studies, we examine latent-preference discovery, personalized preference alignment, and the externalization of vague, difficult-to-express creative intentions.

title: Causal Humility: Governing the Authority of Fairness Claims Under Causal Uncertainty
summary:
AI systems increasingly shape consequential decisions in employment, lending, healthcare, and public services, making fairness an important problem for auditing and governance. Fairness assessment often requires more than identifying disparities in outcomes; it also requires understanding how those disparities arise. Causal approaches to algorithmic fairness address this explanatory problem by representing pathways through which protected attributes and other factors may influence outcomes. Yet causal reasoning in sociotechnical systems remains uncertain: relevant confounders may be unobserved, causal directions contested, and conclusions sensitive to modeling assumptions and representational choices.
  We introduce causal humility as a governance framework for managing the relationship between epistemic uncertainty and causal authority. Drawing on causal fairness research, epistemology, political philosophy, and science and technology studies, causal humility has four requirements: making consequential assumptions and omissions visible; preserving contestability across defensible causal accounts; recognizing indeterminacy as a legitimate analytical outcome; and maintaining proportionality between evidentiary support and institutional authority or action.
  We operationalize these requirements through Causal Cards, a documentation artifact for recording the causal basis, assumptions, omissions, model dependence, and governance implications of fairness claims. Using the UCI Adult dataset as a worked epistemic demonstration, we show how different causal discovery procedures applied to the same observational data render fairness-relevant pathways visible, absent, or unresolved. Causal humility treats such disagreement as information about the limits of what can responsibly be claimed and the authority those claims should carry.

title: SPIDES: Information-Flow Control for Browser Agents
summary: Browser agents automate complex workflows by reading and acting on arbitrary page content, but this flexibility exposes them to prompt injection attacks and unintended data exfiltration. Recent work argues that LLM-driven browser agents erode traditional web security boundaries such as the Same-Origin Policy (SOP) by acting across origins with the user's authority and no built-in isolation. We argue that restoring SOP is neither sufficient (a same-origin public sink can leak private data) nor necessary (legitimate tasks require authorized cross-origin flows) for protecting the security of users. We propose SPIDES, which instead enforces information-flow control by gating primitive browser actions such as typing, clicking and navigating on labels propagated from element-level HTML confidentiality and integrity annotations. Untrusted and confidential content is masked from the agent's context, while policies block unauthorized flows, providing security guarantees against both prompt injection and data exfiltration that hold independently of the model driving the agent. To evaluate SPIDES and baseline defenses under a common threat model, we build MicroNet, a closed ecosystem of 28 interlinked websites with element-level ground-truth labels and paired benign/adversarial tasks. SPIDES achieves 0% attack success rate by design while retaining high task completion rate and autonomy. Our findings demonstrate that information-flow control is an effective technique to extend web security to browser agents, gaining on autonomy and utility against state-of-the-art baselines. The source code and data are openly accessible at https://github.com/microsoft/SPIDES.

title: VERAS: Verification-Guided Adaptive Search for Reliable Operations Research
summary: Advances in reasoning, coding, and tool use enable LLM agents to solve operations research (OR) problems through iterative problem modeling, program construction, and verification. Yet passing self-authored verification does not ensure that the solutions satisfy task constraints and meet optimization quality. This gap can arise from correlated specification errors, where the generated program and its checks share omissions or misinterpretations of task requirements, alongside incomplete verification coverage and ineffective optimization strategies. We propose VERAS, a verification-guided adaptive search harness for reliable OR that uses verification evidence to prioritize feasibility repair, constraint-coverage review, and solution-quality improvement. VERAS combines task-specific solution checkers with a separate verification agent to examine candidate solutions against the task requirements. It uses verification feedback to guide feasibility repair, additional constraint checking, and objective improvement, while candidate acceptance criteria screen revisions for deterioration in output validity or constraint satisfaction. On ORAgentBench, VERAS achieves a 42.99% pass rate, exceeding the reported 35.51% of Codex using the same LLM. Across two industrial-scale OR problems, VERAS reduces inter-datacenter peak bandwidth by 10.34% relative to native Codex and lowers annualized distribution network planning costs by 6.28% compared with expert-designed solutions. Code and evidence are available at https://github.com/holimario/VERAS.

title: YouTube Clips and Broad but Shallow Attention to Candidates: Evidence from the 2024 Tokyo Gubernatorial Election
summary: Video-sharing platforms and social media have gained influence in election campaigns, and third-party edited videos (called kirinuki in Japanese; hereafter, "clip videos") in particular have attracted attention. In Japan, Shinji Ishimaru, previously unknown nationally, finished second in the 2024 Tokyo gubernatorial election, a result widely attributed to his popularity on YouTube. Focusing on this case, we analyzed 44,331 YouTube videos relating to the nine leading candidates, posted between July 5, 2020, and July 7, 2024. Using cumulative views and engagement data as of June 25, 2025, we examined the relationship between clip videos and the attention candidates received. Regression analyses with standard errors clustered by channel showed that Ishimaru, the most watched candidate, did not draw the most active engagement. Videos mentioning Ishimaru received about 36% fewer likes and 41% fewer comments at the same number of views, whereas some candidates with fewer views recorded higher engagement rates. Clip videos were associated with this breadth of attention. They received about 1.8 times more views but 26% fewer comments at the same number of views, and mentions of Ishimaru were associated with about 2.6 times more views among non-clip videos. The interaction between the two, however, was not significant, and understanding the prominence of Ishimaru's cumulative views requires considering both the number of clip videos about him and the views per video. These results suggest that the spread of attention through clip videos may have functioned as a broad but shallow pathway, distinct from the formation of committed support.

title: Zero-Shot Tabular Learning via Hypergraph Reasoning with LLMs
summary: Tabular data are prevalent across diverse domains such as healthcare and finance. Zero-shot tabular learning aims to make predictions without labeled data. However, existing LLM-based approaches rely on row-wise prompting, resulting in high inference cost and limited use of inter-row dependencies. In this work, we propose TABHGR+, an efficient relation-aware zero-shot framework for tabular data that leverages LLM-generated rules to label and group rows. Specifically, based on column and task descriptions, we use LLMs to generate rules that assign weak labels to all rows. To refine these noisy weak labels, we construct a hypergraph by grouping semantically related rows using LLM-generated rules and perform hypergraph-based label propagation. Lastly, we further enhance the LLM-generated hypergraph for propagation, which is potentially sub-optimal, by assigning label-adaptive weights to hyperedges. By requiring only a constant number of LLM calls independent of dataset size, TABHGR+ substantially reduces inference cost while achieving higher classification accuracy than zero-shot and strong few-shot baselines.

title: Unified Multiparadigm Fusion Intelligence for Rare Disease Diagnosis
summary: Rare diseases (RDs) affect an estimated 300 million people globally, leaving patients to navigate a protracted diagnostic odyssey constrained by clinical scarcity and fragmented medical knowledge. Artificial intelligence (AI) has progressively advanced RD diagnostics, from symbolic methods and deep learning to large language model (LLM)-based systems. However, each paradigm carries structural limitations: symbolic methods are bounded by knowledge completeness, neural models sacrifice interpretability, and LLM-based systems are vulnerable to evaluation biases like data leakage. In this study, we introduce FusionRare, a unified multiparadigm fusion framework integrating knowledge-driven symbolic reasoning, deep-learning pattern recognition, case-based patient retrieval, and LLM-based heuristic inference via statistical meta-aggregation and knowledge-enhanced agentic reflection. Evaluated on 2,528 strictly isolated clinical cases, FusionRare achieves state-of-the-art RD prioritization, attaining a macro-averaged Recall @1 of 51% for phenotype-only diagnosis and 79% for phenotype-genotype joint analysis. These results represent decisive advantages over the advanced agentic system DeepRare, frontier LLMs including GPT 5.5, and specialized tools like PhenoBrain and LIRICAL under stringent anti-leakage protocols. A randomized, crossover clinician-AI validation demonstrated that FusionRare elevates the true diagnostic rank in 45% of decisions, improves physician confidence in 62%, and reduces time to diagnosis by 21%. These findings indicate that reconciling these orthogonal AI paradigms significantly enhances diagnostic capabilities, bridging the gap between computational benchmarks and actionable clinical reliability. More broadly, this work provides a replicable framework for deploying trustworthy diagnostic AI across complex, high-stakes, and underserved medical domains.

title: When Care Expands and Control Declines: Understanding Digital Privacy in End-of-Life Care
comment: Accepted by IEEE S&P 27, Lionel Z. Wang and Zhuoran Lu are the corresponding authors
summary: Terminally ill patients generate extensive digital health data through hospital portals, physiological monitoring devices, consumer health applications, and end-of-life care platforms. Yet their ability to control this data is systematically undermined by the structural conditions of terminal care. Through semi-structured in-depth interviews with 21 terminally ill patients, 11 family caregivers, and 8 physicians recruited from tertiary hospitals, this study examines the digital privacy circumstances and subjective attitudes of patients in end-of-life contexts. Thematic analysis reveals five structural dimensions of digital privacy challenge: continuous bodily digitization without meaningful informed consent; cognitive decline driving involuntary proxy control of accounts; inferential data generation exceeding patients' epistemic boundaries; dissolution of individual privacy boundaries amid relational network restructuring; and the absence of institutional governance over post-mortem data. Patient privacy attitudes span three profiles: fundamental absence of privacy awareness, sustained active management under severe tool constraints, and perception of problems followed by resigned abandonment. Interviews with caregivers and physicians reveal benevolent substitution in the name of care needs, expansion of access beyond the initial task, and unresolved boundaries under absent institutional guidance. These findings reveal a compounding privacy vulnerability unique to end-of-life contexts and call for privacy-by-design principles, granular permission mechanisms, and institutional governance frameworks tailored to the needs of dying patients.

title: Empirical Analysis of TEE-Enabled Rollup Designs
comment: Accepted for the 24th IEEE International Symposium on Network Computing and Applications, NCA 2026; Copyright is with IEEE
summary: Layer 2 (L2) rollups have become the dominant scaling solution in Ethereum. At the core of these systems lies the rollup sequencer, a component that orders, executes, and submits L2 transaction blocks to the main Ethereum blockchain. The centralization of this sequencer introduces security risks, including censorship and malicious manipulation of transactions to extract maximum extractable value (MEV). Trusted execution environments (TEEs) provide strong hardware-enforced confidentiality and integrity guarantees for code and data. TEEs are strong candidates for strengthening security and ensuring verifiable neutrality in rollup sequencer operations, but multiple TEE-based designs are possible, offering different trade-offs among modularity, performance, and security guarantees. Among them, the separation of proposer and builder logic (PBS) into independent services is a strong contender against the monolithic approach that bundles all sequencer logic. Despite several proposed theoretical frameworks, there is a lack of experimental evaluation of the practicality and security trade-offs of integrating TEEs into rollup sequencers. This work addresses this gap through a comprehensive empirical study of TEE-enabled rollup designs under both PBS and monolithic sequencer models. Our experimental evaluations show that the impact of TEEs on rollup performance is small and that PBS does not significantly amplify it. We also show that PBS can lead to significant performance improvements by enabling more specialized, efficient builder logic implementations.

title: Safety Analysis of CPSs Over-the-air Updates: Test Case Prioritization and Selection
summary: Over-the-air (OTA) updates for Cyber-Physical Systems (CPS) allow engineers to modify their software wirelessly. In the automotive domain, they enable manufacturers to update software without physical access to the vehicle. However, OTA updates can generate a large number of possible software configurations. For example, end users may decide whether or not to install any given OTA updates. The combinatorial explosion of these configurations hampers SW testing, a standard practice for detecting errors in CPS. To overcome this limitation, we propose CRISP (CRIticality-based Selection and Prioritization), a novel framework supporting test case prioritization and selection in the context of OTA updates. Our framework leverages test case robustness, i.e., how far they are from violating the system requirements, to drive test case prioritization and selection. It enables engineers to rank test case executions from most to least critical, and to select only the critical test cases relevant to a given OTA update. We evaluated our approach using a representative SW product line consisting of seven different vehicles, 22 driving scenarios, and two software components. We considered 224 tests, requiring 59 hours of execution time. We assessed the effectiveness of CRISP across five OTA updates. We compared our solution with (a) a random test case prioritization and selection algorithm, and (b) AP-DISC, identified as the state-of-the-art solution in a recent empirical study on the subject. Our results show that CRISP outperforms our baselines in finding failure-revealing test cases, and that our selection procedure can be configured to find reasonable and practical tradeoffs among accuracy (percentage of failure-revealing test cases identified) and computational time (time required to find them).

title: Scam Town: Can Scam Education Spread Like a Vaccine?
summary: Most older adults who hear a warning about scams hear it from someone they know: a relative, a neighbour, or a friend who was targeted. Yet research on scam prevention almost always studies one person at a time. We ask whether scam awareness can spread through a community and protect it the way a vaccine does, since a warning protects whoever hears it and can be passed on. To find out, we built Scam Town, a simulated community in which a large language model plays each resident. Scam centres phone the residents, and after a call a resident can warn the people they know. Word of mouth helped, but it did not take off on its own: each warning led to fewer than one more, so a community cannot count on warnings "going viral". Across 80 simulated towns, everyday talk cut the number of people scammed by roughly a fifth. The largest gains came when an official warning, from a bank, a senior centre, or an agency, reached most of a town and residents then talked about it: in simulation (a combination we did not test live) the two together cut scams by about half. Protection was greatest when warnings reached the people scammers actually call, who here were older residents. Because our residents are language-model stand-ins rather than real people, we treat these findings as predictions to test with people, not as proof. They point to a simple recipe for scam education: give people a clear story they can retell, design campaigns to be passed along, and reach first those most likely to be called.

title: Improving Fake Profile Detection Through Multimodal Learning and Research-Guided Feature Integration
summary: Fake accounts continue to undermine online platforms, yet it remains unclear whether multimodal learning offers meaningful improvements over strong metadata baselines or graph-based approaches. In this work, we study bot detection by integrating textual, visual, and account metadata signals on the TwiBot-22 benchmark using a subsample of 30,000 users. We propose a multimodal framework combining pretrained textual (XLM-RoBERTa) and visual (CLIP) embeddings with structured account-level features such as follower counts, posting frequency, and account age, and evaluate multiple modality combinations using CatBoost alongside a Relational Graph Convolutional Network (R-GCN). Results show that metadata alone is highly predictive, while multimodal fusion yields only marginal and largely statistically insignificant gains. The graph-based model underperforms classical variants under the subsampled graph conditions of this study. Overall, our findings suggest that under practical constraints, feature quality and metadata richness matter more than fusion complexity.

title: LogicVal:A Logic-Formalized Benchmark for Constraint Satisfaction in Text-to-Image Generation
comment: Preprint. Under review. Savitha Sam Abraham and Marjan Alirezaie contributed equally
summary: Text-to-Image (T2I) generative models have made significant progress in producing high-fidelity images from natural-language prompts. Alongside this progress, numerous benchmarks have been developed to evaluate capabilities such as attribute binding, numeracy, spatial reasoning, and commonsense reasoning. In this work, we propose a new perspective on T2I evaluation by casting it as a constraint-satisfaction problem. We introduce a logical framework that formally specifies the benchmark domain, including objects, attributes, and relations, alongside the constraints that generated images must satisfy. We evaluated four state-of-the-art T2I models across 9 classes of constraints ranging from a single-object-attribute to multi-object relationships constraints involving logical operators ($\forall, \exists, count, \rightarrow$). Our results reveal a substantial gap between single-object and complex conditional multi-object relationship constraint classes, with the best-performing model achieving 98% accuracy on the former and just 53% on the latter. We assess compositional generalisation, finding that the best-performing model`s accuracy drops from 84% on single-constraint prompts to 20% when satisfying multiple constraints simultaneously. Identifying unsatisfiable constraints is also challenging, with the best model correctly recognizing only 23% of such prompts. Building on this framework, we introduce \textbf{LogicVal}, an evaluation methodology that combines neural visual detection with logical reasoning to assess constraint satisfaction in generated images. On CLEVR, LogicVal achieves ROC-AUC scores ranging from 0.88 to 0.98, indicating strong alignment with human judgments. These findings underscore the value of logic-based evaluation for characterizing T2I model capabilities and limitations.

title: Exploring Visual Access and Proactive AI Tutoring for Handwritten Mathematics
summary: Handwritten work captures mathematical reasoning that learners may not express in typed or voice-dictated messages. We built a multimodal AI tutoring platform in which a phone camera gives the tutor a live view of learners' work on paper. In a randomized online study, 117 adults solved calculus problems with Text-Reactive, Visual-Reactive, or Visual-Proactive assistance. Analysis of 2,140 tutor messages showed that visual access shifted assistance toward checking ongoing work, while proactivity enhanced error identification and directive hints. Learners valued feedback grounded in their writing; those who received proactive help rated it as supportive, and about a third wanted it more often. These findings inform when tutors should intervene and what they should address. We release the platform, prompts, and instruments, together with 255,984 timestamped images of handwritten work linked to tutoring conversations, intervention decisions, and learning outcomes, to support multimodal tutoring systems that preserve the affordances of handwritten work while providing adaptive feedback.

title: Unbounded Losses, Unchecked Inputs: Measuring the Safeguards of LLM Options-Trading Agents
comment: 26 pages, 9 figures, 8 tables. Original measurement study: a logged screen of 765 GitHub repositories and cell-level scoring of 26 LLM options-trading systems against 18 safeguards
summary: Large language model (LLM) agents now place options orders at retail brokers, and developers publish open-source options agents faster than anyone has examined them. Prior security work on trading agents scored academic equities designs by whether an attacker can flip a buy-or-sell decision. We present the first measurement of the options agents that brokers and developers ship, scored by the safeguards they enforce and by the worst loss their documented order paths can reach. We screened 765 GitHub repositories, broker documentation, and the research literature and found 215 eligible repositories and 8 broker-native agent interfaces. We then scored 26 systems, including every broker interface and every open-source project with at least 20 stars, on seven robustness and eleven security safeguards with cell-level evidence. The ecosystem is new: 198 of the 215 repositories were created in 2026, and 129 (60.0%) appeared in the two weeks around one options-trading hackathon. Of the 22 systems that can place orders, 10 enforce a pre-trade limit outside the model, yet none of the 26 authenticate their text sources or cross-check market data. Of the 26, 17 can execute with no mandatory human step and 13 can reach unbounded loss, including 6 of the 8 broker interfaces. Because an attacker who writes the agent's inputs can move an order's strike, expiry, volatility, and legs while its direction stays correct, options agents need loss limits enforced at the order boundary.

title: Effective Construction of Feature Database of Fingerprinting Functions for Code-Clone SCA
summary:
In contemporary software development, the extensive adoption of third-party libraries has become standard practice to avoid reinventing the wheel. This trend is particularly evident in programming ecosystems that lack mature package managers, such as C/C++. Within this context, Code Clone Detection (CCD) techniques have emerged as essential tools for identifying instances of code reuse, thereby mitigating security and legal concerns. Despite significant advances in CCD algorithms, a notable gap persists between academic tools and real-world applications. This disparity primarily arises because academic tools rely on experimental datasets composed of a limited number of indexed repositories, whereas real-world applications require a much broader scope of code sources.
  To address this challenge, we propose a novel, systematic approach for selecting appropriate open-source repositories to construct a more effective CCD feature dataset. Our method, OSSScope, employs a greedy algorithm to analyze the diversity of fingerprinting functions across 2.55 million C repositories on GitHub, maximizing unique fingerprinting functions while minimizing the number of repositories required. OSSScope compiles an optimal feature dataset containing 61 million fingerprinting functions from 190K repositories, resulting in a 22.65% improvement in recall over SOTA tools, and covers over 95% of the features from other sources. Leveraging the selected repositories, we introduce RClassifier, a lightweight classification model that determines whether a repository should be included, streamlining construction for migration to other language ecosystems. Our evaluation of RClassifier in the Golang ecosystem validates its effectiveness, achieving recall comparable to the dataset produced by OSSScope.

title: A Theoretical Perspective on Link Prediction Heuristics
summary: In network analysis, nodes with different degrees are usually weighted differently in tasks such as link prediction. For example, two individuals connected to the same high-degree node (e.g., a celebrity) are often considered less likely to know each other than if they share a low-degree connection. In this paper, we theoretically justify the reasoning behind this heuristic using a graph generation model. In this model, nodes are embedded in a latent metric space, and edges are more likely to form between nearby nodes. We analytically derive degree-based weighting schemes for commonly used link prediction and similarity measures. In particular, we identify the optimal weighting scheme for the Common Neighbors index and extend our analysis to other popular heuristics, including the graph distance.
